news.title: ‘Disgrace to incarcerate’ Palestinians inside Gaza: US envoy
news.text:
TURMUS AYYA: The US ambassador to Israel has said there is no plan to force Palestinians out of Gaza, after Israeli ministers laid out ideas on how to expel the war-battered territory’s two million people.

“I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will,” Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he visited Palestinian-Americans in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday.

Israeli far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir laid out a plan two days ago that aims to see the departure of 250,000 Pales-tinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of the roughly two million residents over the following six years.

His remarks came a day after Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the population would go.

Huckabee says no plan for forced displacement as Israel bears responsibility for Palestinians’ safety in West Bank

Katz, without citing his source, said 80pc people in Gaza wanted to leave but Hamas was preventing them.

Huckabee said that President Trump’s administration wanted to give Palestinians the option to leave by choice. “There is an open-mindedness if people wish to leave, that they should have the right to leave,” Huckabee said, calling it a “disgrace” to “incarcerate” Palestinians inside Gaza.

“Nobody is suggesting there would be forced displacement — the Israelis are not, the Americans are not. I know of no one who supports that,” he said.

Forced displacement of a civilian population from occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.

Virtually the entire population of Gaza has already been displaced internally by Israel’s military offensive following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

Since the war, some far-right Israeli politicians have spoken of bringing settlers back to the Gaza Strip, where Israel dismantled settlements in 2005 as part of a unilateral plan to disengage from the densely populated region.

The remarks on displacement come in the run-up to the October 27 elections, in which polls show a tight race for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has brought once shunned far-right figures into his cabinet.

US President Donald Trump stunned the world early in his second term by proposing to displace all Palestinians at least temporarily from Gaza and turn the rubble-strewn Mediterranean territory into a luxury resort, but he backtracked after pushback from countries.

Palestinians’ safety

Also, the US ambassador said Saturday that Israel’s government bore responsibility for West Bank Palestinians’ safety and should impose “severe consequences” over violence, as he visited families following a surge in attacks by settlers.

As Mike Huckabee met families inside a finely manicured old house, a settler from a nearby illegal outpost approached in a quad bike.

“One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens,” Huckabee said.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and violence by Israeli settlers towards Palestinian residents has persisted for years, often with little or no legal consequence, but recent months have seen a surge in attacks.

Huckabee stopped short of criticising Israel by name but called for action against the violence, which he insisted was the “work of a small minority of settlers”.

“Our clear message is that crime is crime, terror is terror. When people do it they should have an expectation that they will have severe consequences,” Huckabee said.

He said that taking action was in the “best interest” of Israel.

news.title: Putin, Zelensky order strikes pause amid peace talks
news.text:
Witkoff, Kushner to reach Kyiv today after talks with Putin• Diplomats carrying proposal ‘to end war’

MOSCOW: With both Russia and Ukraine agreeing not to strike each others’ capitals for three days to allow the negotiations to take place, US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held around three hours of late-night talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on ending the war on Saturday, ahead of their first visit to Kyiv on Sunday.

US President Donald Trump has said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing a “proposal” on ending fighting.

Talks ended after just over three hours, past 11pm in Moscow.

The envoys are due on Sunday in Ukraine’s capital for the first time, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War Two.

In televised comments before the closed-door talks began, Putin than-ked Trump for “not stopping” to try to end the war — launchd by Russia in 2022 — despite it being “not simple”.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov earlier said, “The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky —who had offered a truce during the US visits — said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.

“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelensky said on social media.

The Ukrainian leader said the US officials have “already begun working with the Russian side today.”

Earlier, he accused Rus-sia of trying to disrupt their visit with strikes on Kyiv’s two airports, as well as on a civilian target in the Dnipro region that killed five people.

“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” Zelensky said on X.

The envoys are expe-cted in Kyiv on Sunday, a senior Ukrainian official told AFP, while US outlet Axios reported they would meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday.

Trump told reporters the envoys would seek to gauge whether prog-ress towards peace was possible.

“I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They’ve done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it,” Trump said.

The renewed push for dip-lomacy comes as Russia and Ukraine pummel each other with long-range missile and drone attacks.

news.title: Republicans Face Fresh Midterm Warning as Democrats Gain Party Identification Edge
news.text: Republicans are facing a fresh warning ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections, with new Gallup figures showing Democrats holding their strongest advantage in party identification in more than a decade. During the second quarter of 2026, 49 per cent of Americans either identified as Democrats or said they leaned towards the Democratic Party, compared with 39 per cent who identified as Republicans or leaned Republican. The 10-point Democratic advantage matched the margin recorded during the first quarter and was the largest lead for either party in Gallup's quarterly tracking since at least 2015. The figures represent a major shift from the end of 2024, when Republicans and Republican-leaning independents held a 47 per cent to 43 per cent advantage over Democrats. Gallup's data showed that 31 per cent of Americans identified directly as Democrats, while 25 per cent identified as Republicans. Independents accounted for 44 per cent of respondents. The six-point gap between Democrats and Republicans was the widest Democratic advantage in Gallup's measure since the second quarter of 2015. The findings come as Republicans prepare to defend their narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress. Midterm elections traditionally pose challenges for the party occupying the White House, with the president's party often losing congressional seats. Democrats are hoping the current political environment will allow them to regain control of the House and Senate. Analysts, however, caution that party identification alone does not predict election outcomes, as turnout, individual candidates, local issues and the distribution of voters across congressional districts will all play important roles. Other recent surveys have also pointed to a Democratic advantage on the generic congressional ballot. A YouGov/Economist poll found that 36 per cent of US adults would choose a Democratic candidate, compared with 31 per cent for a Republican candidate. A separate Quantus Insights survey of likely voters put Democrats ahead 49.7 per cent to 42.8 per cent on the generic congressional ballot. The same poll showed Democrats leading Republicans 49.3 per cent to 43.4 per cent in a generic Senate ballot. An Echelon Insights survey conducted in August similarly showed Democrats ahead, with 50 per cent of likely voters saying they would definitely, probably or lean towards voting for a Democratic congressional candidate, compared with 45 per cent for Republicans. The polling comes as President Donald Trump's approval ratings, inflation and affordability remain major political issues. Democratic strategists are seeking to turn dissatisfaction with the administration into gains in November, while Republicans are looking to improve their standing before voting begins. Political scientists have stressed that a Democratic lead in national measures does not automatically translate into control of Congress. Republican-friendly congressional maps could limit Democratic gains even if the party performs strongly in the nationwide vote. With the midterms approaching, the latest Gallup figures nevertheless provide another indication of a difficult political landscape for Republicans as they attempt to retain their congressional majorities.
news.summary: Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, new Gallup data reveals a significant Democratic advantage in party identification, with 49% of Americans aligning with or leaning towards the Democratic Party, compared to 39% for Republicans.

news.title: Will the 'bond vigilantes' claim their second British PM? Inside Andy Burnham's high-stakes battle
news.text:
Will the 'bond vigilantes' claim their second British PM? Inside Andy Burnham's high-stakes battle

The bond market sank Liz Truss and now our new PM faces sky-high yields 

See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

By MAGGIE PAGANO

Updated: 00:01 BST, 6 September 2026

In recent years, much has been blamed on so-called ‘bond vigilantes’ – financial hotshots said to be responsible for toppling leaders and dictating policy by selling – or threatening to sell – government bonds.

In Britain, these supposed vigilantes are widely credited with bringing down Liz Truss as prime minister. 

And they are now said to be poised to pounce on Andy Burnham, as concerns about a spendthrift Labour government push the UK’s borrowing costs to their highest level since the 2008 financial crisis.

Unlike their crime-fighting namesakes, bond vigilantes punish governments they regard as fiscally irresponsible.

The term was coined by American economist Ed Yardeni during Ronald Reagan’s presidency in the 1980s to describe investors dumping US Treasury bonds in protest at Federal Reserve policies they believed were inflationary.

Selling bonds drives their prices down, which in turn drives yields, the effective interest rate paid on them, up, making it more expensive for governments to borrow and often forcing a policy rethink.

The vigilantes reappeared during Bill Clinton’s presidency when yields on US ten-year Treasuries climbed above 8 per cent, triggering what was named the Great Bond Massacre of 1994.

It prompted Clinton’s adviser James Carville to remark: ‘If there was reincarnation, I’d like to come back as the bond market. You can intimidate everybody.’

Truss discovered that reality after her September 2022 mini-Budget sparked a sell-off in UK government bonds, known as gilts, sending yields close to 5 per cent and triggering a crisis in the liability-driven investments held by pension funds, prompting an emergency intervention by the Bank of England.

And it is why Burnham received such a roasting in September last year after claiming Britain should not be ‘in hock to the bond markets’, sending 30-year gilt yields to a 27-year high.

The tough task facing Andy Burnham

Now Burnham is Prime Minister, he has softened his language, promising to use ‘any flexibility’ within the fiscal rules. 

But the market is unconvinced. Rising oil prices have reignited global inflation fears, pushing the UK’s ten-year borrowing costs to about 5 per cent, their highest since 2008.

Thirty-year yields reached 5.8 per cent, their highest since 1998.

If Burnham believes nuance will placate the bond vigilantes, many think he is mistaken. 

Anthony Peters, a self-described ‘old bond dog’, argues that in fact there is no such creature as a bond vigilante, adding: ‘It’s far more dangerous than that. The whole gilts market is the vigilante. That’s its job.’

The vigilantes, he says, exist only in the minds of those who believe traders conspire against governments. 

But, he says: ‘It’s got nothing to do with being in hock to the markets. It’s maths. If investors think something bad will happen, they sell.’

The bond market blowout has hit at the worst possible time for the UK: SIMON LAMBERT on why it spells Budget pain

Britain now borrows at higher rates than Portugal, Italy, Greece and even Morocco. 

US bond yields have also soared over worries about America’s budget deficit, triggering the controversial move by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to intervene with a bond buy-back programme aimed at lowering borrowing costs.

However, fighting against the market almost never works – long-dated yields have shot up again.

Yields matter. Servicing the UK’s £3trillion national debt costs £120billion a year. 

So each upward twitch in yields adds to the burden on taxpayers. Keeping yields low is vital, not only to refinance existing debt but for new borrowing.

Why this isn't a Liz Truss moment... yet

Yet if yields are higher than in the Truss chaos, why is there no similar panic? Chris Fellingham, dubbed the City’s gilts king after 40 years of trading, says the market has priced in catastrophe.

‘We are at an impasse until John Healey’s first Budget. The market is treading water,’ he says. ‘Despite all the damaging Budget leaks, we don’t know what they are planning. It’s a game of wait and see.’

Chris Fleming, formerly of Japanese bank Nomura, agrees saying: ‘The markets decide. Right now, no one wants to buy ten-year gilts, let alone 30-year paper. Maybe if yields move closer to 6 per cent they’ll have a nibble. Investors lost confidence after Reeves’ first Budget, and it’s not returned.’

He says we’re seeing a slow-motion crash: ‘Investors don’t see signs of growth. They see only the politics of envy. Bond markets are the best intelligence source you’ll get for where a country’s heading.’

Britain is in a fiscal trap, argues George Cooper at Equitile Investments, saying: ‘Burnham’s trapped by deteriorating public finances, with every extra pound of spending widening the deficit. 

'War bonds are sticking plaster. Underlying the problems is that we’re below population replacement levels. Who will pay for future debt?’

Markets are also increasingly worried about ‘fiscal dominance’ –the point at which investors no longer believe central banks can control inflation through higher interest rates without rendering governments insolvent. 

Faced with that dilemma, Cooper argues, policymakers will ultimately tolerate higher inflation.

What next for the gilt market? 

The gilt market underpins our financial stability. Once dominated by UK pension funds, it has altered dramatically. 

Domestic pension funds and insurers now hold only a third of gilts, while the Bank of England still owns 18 per cent through quantitative easing. Foreign investors control a third, with the rest owned by hedge funds and non-financial corporations, which are becoming more influential.

So where next for gilts? Fellingham says: ‘Healey must convince the markets that Labour will work with the private sector to achieve growth. 

He must set out serious spending cuts in the Budget and maybe a small income tax rise on the middle classes – the rich have been squeezed enough. This could raise £30billion to pay down debt.’

There are even signs among Burnham’s allies that the Government is realising difficult choices must be made to stop the cost of Britain’s borrowing spiralling further out of control.

Mortifyingly for the Prime Minister, Jim O’Neill, his former economic adviser, said the Government must rein in the ‘excesses’ of spending on areas such as the pension triple lock and the welfare system if it is to regain the confidence of bond markets.

Even more embarrassing for the Government, Andy Haldane, former Bank of England economist and now head of the British Chambers of Commerce, and another potential PM adviser, has argued against raising taxes again, saying the UK has reached ‘saturation point’ and that any higher taxes will harm future growth.

And if Healey fails to convince the markets? Fellingham says: ‘If Labour does something stupid like wealth taxes, which will reduce tax revenue and drive more talent overseas, we’re f*****.’

For Burnham, the message is simple: disrespect the bond market at your peril.

news.title: New Acting Army Secretary Says U.S. Troops Should ‘Dominate’ Every Fight
news.text:
“It is now my job,” declares the new acting secretary of the U.S. Army, “to make sure we never send our troops into a fair fight. We will equip them with every cutting-edge advantage needed to completely dominate our enemies and return home safely.”

After the previous Army secretary Dan Driscoll left under a cloud of controversy, President Donald Trump has appointed civilian official Adam Telle as a temporary replacement. Telle was the assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, or the top official at the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and previously for years as a staffer with more than one senator. Trump announced the appointment on Truth Social Thursday, when he called Telle a "Great Patriot," but without providing any details. Telle, however, seems filled with enthusiasm.

Telle posted a little about his background and his vision going forward on X Friday. “I am blessed to have grown up in a small town in the United States of America, living the realization of the promise of America, the Greatest Nation in the history of the world," he said. 

He emphasized the fact that millions of Americans enjoy the fruits of liberty without always remembering the sacrifices that make this possible. "Patriots throughout our nation, from sea to shining sea, enjoy that same precious freedom every day, a miracle that today is too often forgotten. That blessing has been enabled immeasurably by the U.S. Army, which literally built our nation and continues to guarantee those freedoms each passing moment," he stated.

Enthusiastically, Telle insisted, "The U.S. Military is the most powerful, capable, and dynamic entity humanity has ever devised. The Army is its foundational branch, a hardened fighting force that has crushed America's enemies and secured our freedom for 251 years and counting. Americans everywhere are putting their trust in the Army to again meet a pivotal moment in history, and I am grateful that President Trump and Secretary Hegseth understand exactly how high the stakes are."

Read Also: U.S.A. 250: Washington’s Spymaster Surprises and Defeats Long Island Raiders

This year we celebrated America's 250th birthday, but the U.S. Army predates our nation by over a year, founded on June 14, 1775. The Army had been fighting in the field a year before the Continental Congress voted for independence.

Telle is proud to be part of the two and a half centuries of tradition. "To this challenge, I bring my love for our country, deep respect for our service members and their families, and my proven experience rejuvenating a massive, complicated part of the Army," he said, evidently referring to his work with the Corps of Engineers. "Working closely with the Department of War, the Trump Administration, and Congress, we will deliver a more ready and capable Army."

He added, "My previous work in the Army focused on moving at Trump Speed to deliver on one of the Army’s original missions. I will apply that same relentless focus on efficiency to how the Army mans, trains, equips, and modernizes."

Telle ended fervently, “God bless our Soldiers. God bless the U.S. Army. And God bless America!”

news.title: Exclusive – Wagley Says Politicians Let Flock Cameras, Data Centers 'Slide'
news.text:
Louisiana congressional candidate Stephen Wagley said Saturday that career politicians have let data centers and Flock surveillance cameras expand without oversight.

Speaking with host Matthew Boyle on Breitbart News Saturday, Wagley said both issues trace back to a lack of transparency from officials who sign deals with private companies. Wagley, chief operating officer of the Delta College proprietary healthcare-training school, is one of six Republicans running in the state’s open 6th District, with a jungle primary set for November 3.

Wagley said lawmakers have approved data center projects while shielding the terms.

“Our elected officials think it’s okay to sign these NDAs with these private corporations that are basically going to be funded with our tax dollars,” Wagley said. “If they’re signing NDAs, then who are they really representing? Us, or the big companies?”

The Delta College executive said residents cannot see how the projects affect the grid or their bills, pointing to rising costs before the facilities are built.

“Everyone that I’m speaking to is already showing how much higher our electrical costs are getting before the things have even been built,” Wagley said. “We are all for economic growth. We’re all for advancement, but we need transparency.”

The candidate tied the same complaint to Flock cameras, arguing the readers have been abused by some police departments and surveil residents without limits.

“For too long, these career politicians have been signing off on these deals, allocating funds to let things like Flock cameras basically just surveil us nonstop with no oversight,” Wagley said. “People have a right to privacy. It’s out of control.”

The Baton Rouge Republican said he entered politics after a 2014 encounter, when he drove Trump around New Orleans during the then-businessman’s pre-campaign tour.

“Right before he got out of the car, he said, ‘So, you’re a pretty good driver. I don’t think that’s your career. I’ll be looking forward to seeing you in politics one day,'” Wagley said.

Wagley said his campaign has been in talks with the Trump administration and would be “honored” to earn an endorsement, though President Donald Trump has not endorsed in the contest.

Wagley also faulted Congress for failing to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI) said last week that Democrats bear responsibility for blocking the bill, while Trump has floated declaring a national emergency to force voter-ID requirements.

Flock cameras and data centers have surged into midterm races nationwide. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) opened an investigation into the company’s data practices last month, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis ordered license-plate readers pulled from state highways.

Louisiana congressional candidate Stephen Wagley said Saturday that career politicians have let data centers and Flock surveillance cameras expand without oversight.

news.title: Putin meets with US envoys for renewed talks on ending the war in Ukraine
news.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday for talks to try to revive a stalled push to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

President Putin, Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff spoke for more than three hours in closed-door talks that come as both sides continue to escalate aerial attacks. Mr. Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both agreed to pause strikes on each other’s capitals while the talks took place.

Washington’s push to end the fighting has lost momentum as U.S. attention has been focused for the past six months on the Iran war. The last known visit to Moscow by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, was in January, when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.

A first trip to Kyiv for the American emissaries

Both U.S. envoys will also visit Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, for the first time in the peace process on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said.

At the start of the meeting in Moscow, Mr. Putin asked both Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff to pass on his warm wishes and gratitude to President Trump, and described the situation in Ukraine as “not simple.” Russian forces launched an all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.

President Putin "has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russia’s Tass news agency.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Moscow until Monday. He said he spoke on Saturday afternoon with the U.S. delegation after their arrival in Moscow.

"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv," he said.

The U.S. envoys were met at the airport in Moscow by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Tass reported. Mr. Dmitriev shared photos of him meeting with the U.S. delegation as they disembarked, alongside the caption, “Welcome to Moscow Peacemakers.”

Peace process has been at a standstill

With peace efforts stalled, Russia has intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with relentless bombardments stretching into daylight hours, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of air defense systems.

On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv — the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.

The long-range strikes by Ukraine have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs seeking to undermine the Kremlin’s war effort and economy, as well as to make ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.

Zelenskyy links Russian strikes to envoys' visit

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

In a social media post on Saturday, Mr. Zelenskyy said that Russia had carried out overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports, and linked the attack to the planned U.S. visit.

“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” he said.

“We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.”

Russian strikes kill multiple civilians in Ukraine

Russian attacks killed five people and wounded five others at an industrial facility in Ukraine’s southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. He described those killed as employees at the site.

“A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives,” he said.

A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Mr. Hanzha said.

In a statement on Saturday, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as “major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine’s military production.”

The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, Mr. Hanzha said. A service station, supermarket, industrial facility, apartment buildings, and vehicles were damaged. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district.

A Russian drone also struck a house in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, killing at least three people, regional administration head Oleh Syniehubov said.

Two people were killed and another person was wounded in a Russian drone attack on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region on Saturday, local officials said. Earlier on Saturday, head of the regional military administration Tymur Tkachenko said that two people were wounded in an overnight attack on the region.

As of Saturday evening, 28 facilities in five districts of the region had been damaged, Mr. Tkachenko said. These included apartment buildings, warehouses, railway tracks, the territory of an agricultural enterprise, and vehicles, he said.

Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping center in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine’s state emergency services said. 

Emergency crews responding to the attack were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency services said.

Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine’s air force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft — around half of them jet-powered — as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the air force.

In Russia's Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others were wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said in statement that its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.
news.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to try to revive a push to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

news.title: Pete Buttigieg talks unions, Brent Spence Bridge at Labor Day picnic
news.text:
HAMILTON, Oh. — Hundreds of Cincinnati area Democrats gathered at an amusement park on Sept. 5 to hear Pete Buttigieg sketch out his priorities for the country.

Buttigieg, a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, spoke about affordability, gerrymandering and the Brent Spence Bridge at the Labor Day picnic sponsored by the Cincinnati AFL-CIO Labor Council.

A crowd clad in campaign t-shirts braved the 87-degree heat, fanning themselves with flyers and Ohio 250 fans, to hear from the former U.S. Secretary of Transportation and other Democratic candidates.

"No better way to spend Labor Day weekend than with the unions who brought us the whole idea of a weekend," Buttigieg said, to cheers and applause at Stricker's Grove.

He spoke about running for office for the first time when he was 27 years old and "no one could say my name” to his time in President Joe Biden's administration.

Buttigieg described the actions of President Donald Trump's administration, such as cuts to food safety officials and the war in Iran and repeatedly said "we can do so much better than that."

Buttigieg mentioned the Brent Spence Bridge project, which he said he checked out earlier in the day.

"You know how important that bridge is to this region and to the economy and to the whole country, and it needed to be fixed for decades, but nobody could make it happen," he said. "Working with leaders like Sherrod Brown and Congressman (Greg) Landsman, and Mayor Aftab, we put $1.6 billion dollars together. We got it done."

Buttigieg said priorities are different for his successor, Trump transportation secretary Sean Duffy, who recently criticized stop-start buttons in cars.

"So if you drive over a pothole on a bridge and it's broken down, paying four bucks a gallon for gas, at least you can do with the old-fashioned key in the ignition," he said.

Landsman, Acton speak at Labor Day picnic

Buttigieg introduced Dr. Amy Acton, who is running for Ohio governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

Acton, who served as the director of the Ohio Department of Health under Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, described herself as a "lifelong public servant."

"I'm a doctor, I’m not a politician. I’m becoming one right before your eyes," she said.

She praised her husband Eric Acton, a public school tacher, and said they would be the "first union family in the governor’s mansion."

Cincinnati Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman, who is facing a tight race for reelection against Republican candidate Eric Conroy, said the No. 1 issue in America is "the extreme concentration of wealth."

He referenced a story from the Bible when Jesus sees merchants in a temple and overturns their tables.

“We need people flipping over tables in America right now,” Landsman said.

Organizers shouted out various Democratic candidates, including Sherrod Brown, who organizers said was unable to attend the picnic this year, and Vanessa Enoch, who is running against U.S. Rep. Warren Davidson.

news.title: Russian President Affirms Commitment to Ensuring Security of Ukraine Settlement Talks
news.text:
Moscow, September 05 (QNA) - Russian President Vladimir Putin asserted Saturday that his country will do everything that would ensure the security of negotiations to find a solution to the conflict with Ukraine.

 During his meeting with US President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow, Putin revealed that the Ukrainian side has been largely reducing its strikes on Russian territories since midnight today.

 The Russian armed forces haven't launched any strikes on Kyiv since that time, Putin noted, a move Moscow described as a "partial truce" that has been agreed upon through channels of security apparatuses.

 Despite his awareness of the formidable situation, Putin said he would remain relentless when it comes to stepping up efforts to reach a settlement and help resolve the Russian-Ukrainian conflict.

 Putin added that Moscow received a proposal to temporarily cease strikes on Kyiv through official channels of intelligence apparatuses and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, stating that the Ukrainian side propounded a three-day broader truce, whilst this pitch hadn't been directly discussed between Moscow and Kyiv.

 The Kremlin announced earlier today that President Vladimir Putin had ordered a three-day halt to strikes on Kyiv, concurrently with the US envoys' visit and talks on resolving the conflict with Ukraine.

 US President Donald Trump had indicated that the envoys would present a peace proposal during their visit to Moscow aimed at ending the conflict in Ukraine.

 This sixth-of-its-kind meeting between Putin and the US interlocutors comes amid extensive diplomatic efforts to make a breakthrough in the Ukrainian issue and find a panacea for the Russian-Ukrainian conflict, as both envoys are scheduled to head to Kyiv on Sunday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (QNA)

news.title: John Healey urged to boost funding for Armed Forces amid renewed fears for Falklands defence as tensions over territory escalate
news.text:
Chancellor John Healey has been told that renewed threats to the Falkland Islands' security have highlighted the urgent need to boost funding for the Armed Forces.

As Mr Healey prepares to deliver a speech on Monday to try to reassure jittery markets over Labour's stewardship of the economy, military experts warn that Britain will have 'major problems' defending the islands if Argentina repeats its 1982 invasion.

Tensions over the territory have escalated after Argentinian president Javier Milei reiterated the country's claim on the Falklands and moved to enforce a crackdown on oil exploration in the area.

This came after US President Donald Trump said that US support for the UK over the issue was 'under review'.

Britain's contingency plan to reinforce the islands is to send troops and helicopters by Airbus A400M from RAF Brize Norton. The only other option is to emulate Margaret Thatcher's naval Task Force, which would rely on an escort from Nato submarines.

But Tim Ripley, a senior military analyst at Defence Eye, said: 'The UK military is not prepared for war in the Falklands, it has just enough capability to defend the garrison until it can be reinforced. 

The problem is if Argentina attacks the runway, we would have major problems getting troops to the South Atlantic Ocean. We have no military helicopters in the Falklands [and] no frigate and submarine has been in the area in years.' 

He added: 'Argentina could easily land on one of the uninhabited islands in the west and claim sovereignty in an asymmetric-style assault that we would struggle to react to.'

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: 'It is madness for Labour to spend billions on welfare for people with mild mental health conditions who could be working, while our Armed Forces are crying out for more funding to defend this country including the Falklands. We look weak and our enemies are sniffing the opportunity. Healey needs to get a grip, cut the welfare bill and put Britain's national security first.'

The Mail on Sunday's Don't Leave Britain Defenceless campaign has been pushing Labour to find more money for the Armed Forces and security of the nation. 

Mr Healey is expected to use his speech to try to calm the markets after borrowing costs hit their highest level in 28 years. A Treasury source said 'fiscal discipline' and plans to secure economic growth would be 'an important part of his message'.

Mr Healey quit as defence secretary and effectively finished Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year after the then-PM failed to commit to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030. He accused the Treasury of being 'unwilling' to 'commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country'.

At Reform UK's conference on Saturday, Robert Jenrick said Nigel Farage would 'crush' Argentina if it tried to take the Falklands and use 'every lever of the British state' to defend the islands if he was PM.

The Falklands' garrison comprises 120 infantry soldiers, four Typhoon jets and the air defence system Sky Sabre, which has a limited number of missiles due to the perceived 'low threat' from Buenos Aires.

A key guardian of the Falklands has been a Royal Navy nuclear submarine and, until 2024, a sub was routinely deployed to the South Atlantic. 

But delays with Astute-class attack subs and maintenance issues have left the fleet unable to send a sub. The lack of a frigate also prevents troops from patrolling South Georgia – where the 1982 war began.

In the past year, Argentina has beefed up its armed forces with the purchase of 24 US-made F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft from Denmark and advanced armoured vehicles from Washington.

But a Ministry of Defence spokesman said: 'These claims [by military experts] are baseless. We are more than capable of defending the Falkland Islands and we stand ready to protect the Islanders' freedom and self-determination.'

news.summary: Chancellor John Healey will deliver a speech on Monday to try to reassure jittery markets over Labour's stewardship of the economy.

news.title: Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff meet Putin and speak for more than three hours in top secret talks... as Russian president gives two-word summation of Ukraine war
news.text:
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff spent over three hours in top-secret talks with Vladimir Putin amid the White House's renewed bid to end the war in Ukraine.

The US envoys landed in Moscow on Saturday morning and were escorted by the Russian President's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, to the Kremlin.

Putin met with Witkoff and Kushner for closed-door talks where he described the conflict as a 'complicated situation,' but praised his American counterpart for wanting to end the war.

'Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,' Putin said of Trump.

Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both agreed to pause strikes on each other's capitals while the talks took place.

'Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,' presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russia's Tass news agency.

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Moscow until Monday. He said he spoke on Saturday afternoon with the US delegation after their arrival in Moscow.

'From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,' he said.

Washington's push to end the fighting has lost momentum as US attention has been focused for the past six months on the Iran war. 

'I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it,' Trump said.

'They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war,' he said.

Witkoff and Kushner last visited Moscow in January, when they also held talks with Putin at the Kremlin.

Both US envoys will also visit Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, for the first time as part of the peace process on Sunday, Ukrainian officials said. 

Russian forces invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

Ahead of the envoys' arrival, Putin's deputy foreign minister warned the US about how to bring the four-year war to an end.

'The key question ​is the extent ⁠to which ⁠the US administration is prepared to invest in ‌finding a real solution to the current crisis, considering ‌the realities on the ground,' Sergei Ryabkov said.

This, according to Ryabkov, was a situation not developing in Kyiv's favor, Russian state news agency TASS reported.

It comes as Zelensky announced today that Russia carried out 'deliberate' strikes on Ukrainian airports overnight in Kyiv and Boryspil.

'Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,' he wrote on X.

'We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.

'Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side. Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer. Russia will be held accountable for what it does.'

The Ukrainian president added that four people were killed and five others injured after a Russian strike in Kamianske, in the Dnipro region.

The Daily Mail contacted the White House for comment.
news.summary: The US envoys landed in Moscow on Saturday morning and were escorted to the Kremlin for talks with Putin behind closed doors.
news.author: Editor,Rachel Bowman

news.title: Greens pile pressure on NHS over use of tech giant... even though it has helped to speed up cancer diagnoses
news.text:
Zack Polanski's Green activists are using their growing influence in local authorities to put pressure on the NHS to stop the use of Palantir software – despite evidence it has cut waiting lists and fast-tracked cancer diagnoses.

The US tech giant, which has won a total of £600 million in public-sector contracts, has been targeted by Left-wing activists for its work with Donald Trump's immigration authorities and the Israeli military.

A break clause in the company's £330 million seven-year NHS contract would need to be exercised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham by the end of this year.

The Greens have joined forces with Labour, the Liberal Democrats and Left-wing groups such as Amnesty International to put pressure on local NHS Trusts, with Sheffield, Rotherham and East Hertfordshire councils all bringing near-identical motions against Palantir in recent months.

Sheffield is run by a formal Labour-Green joint administration while East Hertfordshire District Council is run by a Green and Liberal Democrat coalition.

The Rotherham motion, introduced in July, urged the council to call on the Rotherham NHS Foundation Trust to pause expansion of Palantir technology. 

It was brought by Independent councillor Taiba Yasseen and seconded by Green councillor Mick Bower, with Labour support. 

Greens on Coventry City Council also forced through a motion on the council's own contract with Palantir, which is used to help social workers in the area.

Mr Polanski wrote to Palantir's chief executive in January demanding the firm 'pack its bags and get the hell out of the NHS'.

A Palantir spokesman said: 'This activity risks denying patients access to technology that can improve the care they receive. 

'Since our software has been rolled out, NHS trusts using it have recorded 110,000 additional operations, a 15 per cent reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients, and a 6.8 per cent average improvement against the NHS's 28-day Faster Diagnosis Standard.'

Palantir's UK chief executive, Louis Mosley, has previously said that the company 'should be judged on whether we are delivering for patients in this country'.

news.summary: The US tech giant, which has won a total of £600 million in public-sector contracts, has been targeted by Left-wing activists.

news.title: REVEALED: Rare agreement between FF and FG Cabinet ministers ahead of next month's Budget will be welcome news for cash-strapped households as winter closes in... but environmental lobby won't be pleased
news.text:
The Cabinet has agreed that proposed carbon tax rises in next month's Budget are now 'politically impossible'.

Ministers this weekend confirmed there will be ‘no Government-initiated’ increases to home heating fuel, petrol or diesel while oil prices remain in turmoil due to the escalating conflict with Iran.

There is a growing consensus at the top of Government that a more permanent, budgetary solution is needed to confront spiralling fuel costs – not least because of the increasing political damage it is inflicting on the Coalition parties.

As US President Donald Trump – who will visit Ireland next weekend – finds himself increasingly stuck in the Middle East quagmire and oil prices show little sign of receding in the near future, the Coalition continues to pursue a strategy of short-term fuel price suppression.

At home, rising prices at the pumps caused by the continuing deadlock in the Strait of Hormuz have fuelled fears of further protests and political instability.

However, temporary suspension of taxes and suspension of fuel excise increases are extremely costly to the Exchequer, and there is increasing pressure coming from rural Government backbenchers – and even ministers – to deal with long- term fuel costs.

Carbon tax on home heating oil is due for a scheduled rise in the middle of next month after the October 6 Budget, but the MoS has learned this will not now go ahead.

The schedule of carbon tax rises planned for between now and 2030 are also being looked at.

The Coalition has already suspended the reimposition of motor fuel excise until at least next year.

A Cabinet source told the MoS: ‘These carbon tax measures were agreed in another world, before the war in Iran. Of course, some in government received a fright from the impact of the fuel protests, but ultimately this is about protecting the public, and centrist voters, from the long-lasting damage of rising fuel costs.

‘While hugely conscious of the environmental challenges, we simply accept that it is politically impossible for the proposed carbon tax increase to be imposed next month.

‘Similarly, we are cognisant that monthly eruptions of cuts on fuel is not a long-term strategy. We, in Cabinet, are discussing longer term solutions.’

Another Cabinet source said the proposed carbon tax increases will ‘100 per cent not happen in October or in the short term’.

The move to temporarily shelve carbon taxes is likely to spark a backlash from environmental groups and comes after United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres this week warned ‘humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe’. Mr Guterres was speaking after a landmark UN report warned

global warming levels will soon overshoot the 1.5 degree target.

And writing in today’s MoS, Prof Peter Thorne, one of the country’s foremost climate change experts, said people will pay a heavy economic – and environmental price – if the Government ditches the

carbon levies, which he describes as ‘the most progressive and transparent tax in the land’.

However, ministers and TDs from rural constituencies who spoke to the MoS this weekend said there is increasing internal discussion of advances made by groups such as Independent Ireland based upon their better perceived understanding of challenges facing rural voters.

Finance Minister Simon Harris and Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers are also coming under pressure for a package to assist rural pubs.

After last year’s Budget, carbon tax on petrol and diesel is €71 per tonne of carbon dioxide emitted. For other fuels, including home heating oil, the current rate of carbon tax of €63.50 per tonne had been scheduled to rise to €71 per tonne on October 14.

But senior Cabinet sources say the planned carbon tax rises will not now go ahead. Ministers said they are also listening to colleagues, particularly those from rural Ireland, who are urging a longer-term fix.

Minister for State at the Department of Agriculture and Limerick County TD Niall Collins, who represents a primarily rural constituency, told the MoS: ‘The establishment in Dublin doesn’t fully understand the effects that rising fuel costs have on those like our constituents in rural Ireland.

‘Obviously, we don’t have access to mass transit, and in so many areas use of a car is the only option for getting to work, school, leisure activities and everything else.’

Speaking after it was confirmed this week that corporation tax payments are up 8.3 per cent to €17.8billion this week, Mr Collins added: ‘Those working families I speak to look at our most recent corporate tax take and they see that the levels of taxes coming into our Exchequer is comparable to the levels you’d see in a country that had struck oil.

‘The Government is investing these tax takes in infrastructure and long-term funds, but there must be some type of longer-term solution to fuel inflation. That may well be done in the Budget.’

Ministers concede Ireland has some of the highest fuel tax rates in the EU, ranking fifth most expensive for petrol and third for diesel among members states.

However, corporation tax payments shot up by 32.5 per cent last month to €2.8billion compared to August 2025, partly due to some large multinationals being charged a higher rate of tax.Multinationals with turnover of more than €750million are now taxed at 15 per cent instead of the lower rate of 12.5 per cent as part of measures to clamp down on tax avoidance.

The decision to suspend the restoration of excise on motor fuel saw excise down 17.4 per cent at €428million.

It has fallen 7.1 per cent so far this year to €3.9billion.

However, ministers and TDs believe this drop can be balanced by corporation tax receipts that give Ireland a tax take that is equivalent to – in the word of one Cabinet source – an ‘oil strike’.

There are also growing fears among Fine Gael – and particularly Fianna Fáil – rural TDs that seats will be lost to Independent Ireland in the next General Election.

Government TDs warned rival rural candidates will be giving a ‘Fianna Fáil narrative on fuel costs and issues like rural pubs at the next election that we should be giving’.

One Fianna Fáil TD told the MoS: ‘We can, of course, do more than provide a narrative. We have control of this at the moment, and we need to move quickly to start building up to the general election.’

The Fuels for Ireland industry group yesterday said the wholesale price of diesel has risen by 15 cent in the last week alone as thousands of hauliers and transport operators from across the country attended the second day of the Irish Road Haulage Association’s (IRHA) annual conference in Killarney, Co. Kerry.
news.summary: As Donald Trump finds himself stuck in a Middle East mess and oil prices soar, the Coalition continues to pursue a strategy of short-term fuel price suppression.
news.author: Editor,John Lee

news.title: Donald Trump's Tariff Policy Has Repeatedly Triggered Multi-Trillion-Dollar Stock Swings Since Early 2025. Here's Why Markets Still Struggle to Price In His Next Move.
news.text:
President Donald Trump is proving to be a very challenging commander-in-chief to work around for most investors, even as markets have soared during his tenure. On April 3, 2025, the day after the much-hyped "Liberation Day" barrage of new tariffs, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.38%) fell 4.8% as the Magnificent Seven group of technology companies corrected sharply downward.

Just six trading days later, most of the damage had been erased, leaving investors with whiplash and prompting many to wonder whether they'd sold their assets too hastily. Volatility never went away, but it now concentrates in individual stocks rather than the market as a whole. The gap between average single-stock volatility and index volatility hit an all-time high of 31% in early July 2026, according to CBOE Global Markets. Therein lies the crux of why markets are still struggling to get a read on what the president is going to do next.

A single social media post from Trump vaporized $2 trillion of market value in one day

U.S. tariff policy has changed more than 50 times since January 2025, according to the Tax Foundation. In most of those cases, investors learned about the policy changes via a social media post from the president. The market's moves with each new change have frequently rivaled past stock market crashes in size.

For instance, Nike crashed 14% on April 3, 2025, and Apple declined by 9%. Both crashes were caused by the companies' heavy reliance on supply chains in Asia, which were hit by the new tariffs. Then, on April 9, 2025, Trump waived the initially declared tariff rates for 90 days, causing Apple to bounce by 15.3%. The S&P 500 itself had its best day since 2008.

Months afterward, on Oct. 10, the president threatened a large tariff increase on Chinese goods, then set a new 100% tariff rate to take effect on Nov. 1. Roughly $2 trillion of American stock market value vanished that afternoon. Three weeks later, after a high-profile meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the increases were scrapped.

Adaptation is extremely difficult here

The market is caught in a pickle regarding the Trump administration's chaotic approach to announcing and implementing new trade policies.

The president's statements cannot be taken literally, nor can they be taken as predictive of the policies that will actually be implemented. Given the nature of trade policy negotiations, his public statements must be considered part of a bargaining process. Tariffs can also be waived for some or all of the affected stakeholders. Apple won an exemption from the 100% semiconductor tariff in August 2025.

At the same time, the market can't ignore or fully discount the administration's statements. Haphazard as the tariff policies may be, the president is the head of government, and the government thus reacts to his dictates, even if they're ill-advised or contradictory.

This is the reason for the volatility. The market has no choice but to believe today that Trump's preferences will translate into real policy, even though it might not.

So far, it looks like the best approach for investors is to take advantage of downside volatility when it arrives, and load up on quality names when they're valued at a panic discount.
news.summary: The president's unique approach to trade policy is creating a lot of volatility.
news.author: Alex Carchidi

news.title: German rocket reaches space as Europe enters satellite launch race
news.text:
German start-up Isar Aerospace on Saturday launched its first rocket into space from a site in Arctic Norway, bringing Europe closer to offering satellite flights from its own soil.
The uncrewed Spectrum rocket was the first commercial flight to reach orbit from continental Europe, ‌where several nations have said they want a share of a growing market for space missions.
“We’re in orbit! And just made European history,” Isar said in a post on social media.
The event was a breakthrough for the European launch industry, giving the continent better access to space, Norway’s minister of industry and commerce, Cecilie Myrseth, said in a statement.
“The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoeya strengthens Norwegian and ⁠European security in the turbulent times we live in,” Myrseth said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Isar’s launch site in ‌March, underscoring Europe’s efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the United States is shifting under US President Donald Trump.
Blasting off from Norway’s Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, ‌the uncrewed Spectrum, designed for small and medium-sized payloads, carried five small satellites as well as an ⁠in-flight technological experiment, according to ⁠Isar.

It was Isar’s second launch, coming 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle soon after ‌take-off from the same site. No one was injured at the time.
The March 2025 launch was nonetheless deemed a success by the company for generating large ‌amounts of ‌data for its developers, it said at the time.
Saturday’s launch was intended as “both the vehicle’s qualification mission and its first flight ‌carrying payload”, the Bavarian company has said.
Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the ⁠United States, and French ArianeGroup, a joint venture between Airbus and Safran that uses a spaceport in South America’s French Guiana.
SpaceX, ⁠a company spanning rockets, satellites and AI, listed on the Nasdaq exchange in June in a record initial public offering.
Sweden, with its Esrange launch site, and Britain with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, ‌are the nearest rivals to the ‌Norwegian site, all of which aim to give Europe greater autonomy in space flights.
Isar said last week it had secured about €200 million (US$232 million) from the European Space Agency to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure.
The German company is also developing a second launch site in Canada.

news.title: US Envoys Head To Kyiv After  Stop In Moscow, Late-Night Meeting With Putin
news.text:
KYIV -- After a day of crucial meetings in Moscow, including with President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are switching wartime venues, heading to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy with aims of ending the conflict now in its fifth year.

Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reported that talks between the envoys and Putin lasted about three hours, with the US representatives leaving the Kremlin at about 11 p.m. on September 5. Shortly after midnight, TASS reported the Americans had departed Moscow.

Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, who participated in the session, called the talks "substantive, very frank, and constructive." He added that the envoys stated the US position and promised to present Putin's views to Ukrainian leaders during their talks in Kyiv.

"They not only expressed their traditional interest in bringing the hostilities to a quick end, they put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," he said.

Ushakov insisted Russia would achieve its goals and that the "root causes" of the conflict must be resolved, Kremlin code for putting an end to Ukraine's hopes of NATO membership and steps to effectively disarm the Ukrainian military, among other historical grievances -- items Kyiv has long rejected.

There was no official US comment immediately after the meeting.

As the session started near 8 p.m., RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their Kremlin discussions.

The meeting appeared to get a late start after Putin spent the day opening a new subway line in Moscow, inaugurating a Siberian oil terminal by video link, and meeting with members of the ruling United Russia party.

US President Donald Trump had said the envoys would be presenting a peace deal to the Russians and then would relay the offer to Ukraine the next day.

Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on September 4.

'Diplomatic Activities

Zelenskyy said he had spoken to the envoys on September 5, revealing few details about the call but saying that "the plan of diplomatic activities for tomorrow in Kyiv with the participation of the American team has been approved."

"We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a meaningful conversation," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and come amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.

Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive, and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.

Reflecting the hard-line stance put forward by Ushakov, Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.

Before the envoys departed the US, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.

Following his September 5 call with the envoys, Zelenskyy said that "from now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow."

Putin subsequently ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8, according to spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who made no mention of other parts of Ukraine amid reports that Russia had continued its attacks elsewhere.

Airport Attacks

Zelenskyy said Russian forces had targeted Kyiv's Zhulyany and Boryspil airports overnight on September 4-5, accusing Moscow of seeking to create uncertainty over the US envoys' planned journey to Ukraine.

The Kyiv visit will come just days after a Russian drone strike hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service -- known as the SBU and a key agency that would be responsible for the US envoys' safety during a visit.

"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said on X , adding there would be "no threats to diplomacy" from the Ukrainian side.

Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.

With reporting by Reuters and AFP
news.summary: After a day of crucial meetings in Moscow, including with President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are switching wartime venues, heading to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy with aims of ending the conflict now in its fifth year.
news.author: Rfe/rl's Ukrainian Service

news.title: Putin Meets US Envoys as Russia Halts Strikes on Kyiv for 72 Hours
news.text:
A three-day pause on strikes in Russia and Ukraine’s capital cities began on Saturday as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow to mediate peace talks between the two countries.

Russian President Vladimir Putin confirmed on Sept. 5 that he ordered a 72-hour pause on strikes in Ukraine’s capital city, Kyiv, as the U.S. special representatives planned to journey from Russia to Ukraine over the weekend as they work to broker a deal to help end the war, which escalated in February 2022.

The U.S. envoys arrived at Moscow’s ​governmental airport on Saturday and were greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who shared photos of the arrival in an X post with the caption, “Welcome to Moscow Peacemakers @SteveWitkoff and @jaredkushner!” The post included a dove emoji at the end.

Witkoff and Kushner then met with Putin on Saturday at the Kremlin.

Putin opened the talks by admitting that the process would not be simple, then sent his “best wishes and words of gratitude” to U.S. President Donald Trump, according to a translated transcript of the meeting provided by the Kremlin.

“While he understands that he’s entering a difficult situation overall, he’s not stopping his efforts to resolve and contribute to the resolution of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,” Putin said, while speaking about Trump during Saturday’s meeting. “Today, we'll discuss all its components, all aspects, and we, for our part, are ready to inform you of our view of the situation.”

Putin said he’s comfortable working with Witkoff and Kushner, saying “the level of trust we have in this process is certainly quite high.”

On Sunday, the two U.S. envoys will meet with officials in Kyiv, which was confirmed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process,” Zelenskyy wrote in an X post on Sept. 5.

“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv.”

Zelenskyy added that he is ready for a “substantive conversation.”

A separate ceasefire, brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency, was underway on Saturday at the ‌Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine.

The pause in fighting was made to allow repairs to restore external power to the plant, which has relied on emergency ​diesel generators to cool its vital safety systems since Aug. 20.
news.summary: U.S. special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
news.author: Jacki Thrapp

news.title: Trump’s MAGA Group Launches $10 Million Ad Blitz in Texas Senate Race
news.text: President Donald Trump’s political group, MAGA, Inc., is spending $10 million on television and digital advertisements in the Texas Senate race, marking its first major investment in a high-profile general election contest ahead of the 2026 midterms. The spending was disclosed in a filing with the Federal Election Commission on Saturday and comes as Republicans face growing concerns about the competitiveness of the traditionally Republican state. Democratic state Representative James Talarico, 37, is challenging Republican nominee Ken Paxton for the Senate seat. Trump endorsed Paxton, helping him defeat incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff in May. The president has continued to support Paxton despite concerns over the candidate's public controversies and his appeal to voters. The $10 million advertising campaign focuses heavily on taxes, seeking to portray Talarico as a candidate who would raise taxes on Texans. The advertisements highlight his support for higher taxes on wealthier households while suggesting that Paxton would provide tax breaks for first-time homebuyers and families with children. Talarico’s campaign has rejected the claims, accusing groups supporting Paxton of misrepresenting his record. Campaign spokesperson JT Ennis said Talarico had supported a major property tax cut in Texas and had consistently backed tax reductions for working Texans. The Texas race has taken on added significance as Republicans attempt to defend their congressional majorities. Public concerns over inflation, the economy and the war with Iran have created political challenges for Trump and Republican candidates ahead of the November elections. MAGA, Inc. has at least $400 million in campaign funds available, creating expectations that Trump will spend heavily in competitive races. Trump said Friday that he would spend whatever amount was necessary to help Republican candidates, while stressing that the funds were his to deploy separately from the Republican National Committee. Trump has also acknowledged that Paxton is not necessarily the strongest television candidate, but defended his choice, calling him potentially the best attorney general in the country. The Texas advertising push could signal the beginning of a broader effort by Trump’s political operation to deploy its substantial financial resources in key Senate and House races as the 2026 midterm campaign intensifies.
news.summary: MAGA, Inc., President Trump's political group, is investing $10 million in ads for the Texas Senate race, marking its significant commitment ahead of the 2026 midterms.
news.author: Samannay Biswas

news.title: Donald Trump, 80, Appears to Nod Off Again During Oval Office Event on American Beef
news.text:
President Donald Trump, 80, appeared to struggle to keep his eyes open during a September 4 Oval Office event, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

The president repeatedly blinked and appeared to close his eyes for extended stretches as Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins discussed his latest executive orders aimed at American ranchers and the beef industry.Donald Trump Appears to Fight SleepTrump was seated behind the Resolute Desk alongside Rollins and ranchers from across the country.

As Rollins discussed the orders, Trump appeared increasingly disengaged from the conversation.

With her body turned toward the president, Rollins continued speaking directly to him as he repeatedly blinked and appeared to drift in and out of sleep. 

At one point, Trump closed his eyes while Rollins was talking.'Sleepy Don'Critics ran to social media to poke fun at the sleeping president.

"Sleepy Don is on the job," someone wrote.

"Now we know why Trump called Biden Sleepy Joe as the real sleepy one is himself," a user said.

"Bedtime for Grandpa," another commented.White House Defends Donald Trump's EnergyTrump has faced similar accusations before, including during a White House healthcare briefing where Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Dr. Oz spoke about lowering drug prices. 

During that appearance, Trump was seen with his eyes and mouth appearing to droop while Dr. Oz discussed the cost of medications.

One critic wrote: "It's lights out time for Trump," while another joked, "You would think they’d stop scheduling these press conferences during executive nap time."

A third chimed in: "Let him sleep. He's way more dangerous when he's awake."

The White House has pushed back against previous claims that Trump was sleeping during official events.

"President Trump's sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden's serious mental and physical decline from the American people," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said.

"President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises, and he remains in excellent health," Davis added.Lara Trump Reveals His Sleep ScheduleDuring an appearance on the Planet Tyrus podcast, Lara Trump said the president sleeps only a few hours each night.

"I truly probably do not sleep enough, but I actually kind of find that I'm a little like the president. He sleeps maybe three or four hours a night," she revealed.

"Now, I need a little bit more than that," she continued. "But I think there are some people that can do with less."
news.summary: Donald Trump appeared to nod off again during an Oval Office event on September 4.
news.author: Olivia Salamone

news.title: Another Russian official 'falls' out of window as Putin grows increasingly desperate
news.text: Another high-ranking Russian official has died in mysterious circumstances after reportedly falling from a window - just after stepping down from his post. Colonel Sergei Shalaginov was discovered dead on Tuesday outside an apartment block on Shchorsa Street in Yekaterinburg, roughly 800 miles east of Moscow. The former deputy chief of the Centre for Combating Extremism in the Sverdlovsk region reportedly plummeted from the ninth floor , with blurred images showing a body lying on the pavement below. The strange death adds to a growing list of Russian elites and top businessmen who have plunged out of windows since the invasion of Ukraine began. Conflicting accounts quickly surfaced following the incident. Pro-Kremlin site URA.ru initially claimed Shalaginov died by suicide after a fallout with ministry bosses, but Ukrainian outlet UA.News noted that the article was swiftly deleted. Sverdlovsk Internal Affairs Ministry confirmed the death while denying any internal conflict. Spokesperson Valery Gorelykh claimed Shalaginov had turned down a promotion, dismissed rumors linking the death to his job and called it "an irreparable loss." Local reports from KP-Yekaterinburg and news outlet E1 described him as a well-respected figure who had recently retired, with an unnamed source praising him as "a very good and competent man," adding that he "always fought for his subordinates." The bizarre incident comes as Vladimir Putin faces mounting strain over heavy Russian battlefield casualties in Ukraine. It follows targeted strikes against Russia's oil infrastructure, which have sparked long petrol queues across the country. Desperate to find a way out, peace talks appear to be gathering pace. Kremlin footage released today showed US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner meeting Putin in Moscow. Addressing the negotiators, Putin admitted that the current situation "is not so easy" before promising to explain "how we see the situation." Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for agreeing to a brief three-day pause on capital strikes, ahead of follow-up talks in Kyiv. US President Donald Trump confirmed the envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war."
news.summary: A Russian anti-terror boss has reportedly plummeted to his death from a window, adding to a trail of dead officials as a desperate Vladimir Putin faces pressure
news.author: Liam Randall

news.title: Top US military officials face lie-detectors in leak hunt
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The Pentagon has launched a lie-detector dragnet to comb through high-ranking military officials and identify who leaked information about US munitions stockpiles, according to US press reports.

In July, reports emerged that the United States was rationing munitions — its missile interceptors, in particular — over supply concerns after several months of fighting Iran.

Administration officials vehemently denied those reports, with President Donald Trump saying “we have a lot of ammunition, different types,” while acknowledging that “for some of the more sophisticated stuff, we’d certainly like to have more.” Late Friday, The New York Times reported that some 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff — the Pentagon’s planning and advisory staff — were being required to take polygraph tests as part of an investigation into how classified stockpile information made its way into journalists’ hands.

CBS News later also reported the wide-scale use of lie detectors, while adding that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had not been tested.

Both outlets cited unnamed officials.

Asked by AFP about the reports, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, refused to comment on “internal personnel or investigative matters,” but said that it “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”

“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.

Both the Times and CBS noted the scale of the polygraph testing.

Lie-detection testing is routine during background screenings and security clearance renewals for government staff with access to the most sensitive state secrets.

But the wide-scale deployment of the detectors as part of a leak investigation was rare, if unprecedented, the outlets reported, citing analysts and unnamed officials.
